clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in SLC19A2, encoding a high-affinity thiamine transporter
Classic triad: megaloblastic anaemia, diabetes mellitus and sensorineural hearing loss
The megaloblastic anaemia responds to pharmacological doses of thiamine, unlike vitamin B12 or folate deficiency
Hearing loss is usually permanent and often not reversed by thiamine
Diabetes typically develops in childhood and may partially respond to thiamine early on
The bone marrow shows megaloblastic changes and often ringed sideroblasts
Presentation is usually in infancy or early childhood
reference.pathophysiology: SLC19A2 encodes thiamine transporter 1, which mediates high-affinity cellular uptake of thiamine. Loss of function impairs intracellular thiamine availability in tissues that depend on this transporter, particularly haematopoietic precursors, pancreatic beta cells and the inner ear. Thiamine is a cofactor for enzymes of carbohydrate and nucleic acid metabolism, so its intracellular deficiency impairs DNA synthesis in erythroid precursors (megaloblastic anaemia), beta-cell function (diabetes) and cochlear function (deafness). High-dose thiamine can partially overcome the transport defect through low-affinity routes.
additionalDifferentials: Other syndromic diabetes with deafness (including mitochondrial diabetes)
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film showing macrocytic/megaloblastic anaemia
Bone marrow examination (megaloblastic change, ringed sideroblasts)
Normal serum vitamin B12 and folate
Audiometry and assessment of glucose metabolism
Trial of thiamine with monitoring of the haematological response
redFlags: Severe anaemia requiring transfusion before diagnosis
Additional features such as optic atrophy or cardiac involvement in some cases
reference.prognosis: With early recognition and thiamine supplementation the anaemia and, to some extent, the diabetes can be improved, but sensorineural hearing loss is generally permanent; lifelong follow-up is required.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for ordinary B12 or folate deficiency and missing the transporter defect
Not trialling thiamine in an unexplained childhood megaloblastic anaemia with diabetes and deafness
Expecting thiamine to reverse established hearing loss
Overlooking the diagnosis when only one or two triad features are present initially
management: Lifelong pharmacological (high-dose) thiamine supplementation is the mainstay, correcting the megaloblastic anaemia and often improving early glycaemic control
Manage the diabetes mellitus with insulin as required, recognising that thiamine may reduce insulin needs early in the course
Provide audiological rehabilitation with hearing aids or cochlear implantation, as the sensorineural deafness is usually permanent and thiamine-unresponsive
Monitor the haematological response (full blood count and film) and glycaemic control to titrate thiamine and diabetes therapy
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across haematology, metabolic medicine/endocrinology and audiology
Offer genetic counselling and family screening, as this is an autosomal recessive SLC19A2 disorder
